title: Lens: duplication and reuse
summary: Duplication in Autobots is mostly visible and signposted. Comments name the code that must change together ("as the run list counts it", "see app/layout.tsx", "counted as admit counts it"). Good shared pieces exist: a provider HTTP module, an ownership-checked disposable-stack teardown, an explicit run row-to-DTO mapping, one API error shape, and a harness test that enforces shared form controls. The problem is where sharing stops. In the browser, data access is hand-written at 74 call sites in 31 components, because the generated client's runtime discards error bodies. As a result, 19 error replies are cast instead of parsed, and the paid run-admission request exists in three copies; only one of them disables duplicate submits and keeps its idempotency key after a lost reply. On the server, several rules that guard secrets, money or state have copies that have already drifted apart. The public-text redactor misses the Tavily, Jina and GitHub token families that the log redactor gained under Decision 0017. An approval's return to pending is re-implemented in the GitHub pull-request adapter with its own TTL. The frozen model-policy snapshot has one writer and eight hand-written readers. The run ledger and the "run plus descendants" scope are rewritten in SQL text, with two tree definitions that disagree when delegation is two levels deep. Terminal states, profile names, the offered model set and budget limits are restated across Python, SQL, TypeScript and scripts. Tests and scripts repeat setup heavily: 36 sign-in helpers, 41 check() helpers, 27 blocks that parse a check's output, and 15 disposable-stack lifecycles. Those copies drift too: two leak scans are narrower than the other two, and most output parsers crash instead of recording a failed case. The 8-line detector found 239 file pairs. Its largest cluster, migrations 023 and 027, is the expected forward redefinition of two functions and is not reported.

scores.why: DH-06 asks to avoid duplicated business rules and to use generated types; approval, policy, budget and state rules are copied across layers, and 19 error bodies are cast.

Shared modules exist (provider_http, disposable_db, api-client runtime, contracts/adapters) but stop short: an adapter writes approval state, routes resolve admission policy, and the browser has no data-access module.
Copies swell the largest files: app_db.py repeats its check runner 19 times, the 10k-line Playwright suite repeats signIn 36 times, and 31 components each own their fetch code.

Reusable functions exist but stay local or unused (useLoaded in one file; parseErrorResponse, admitRun and createWorkSession unused in the browser), so the same logic is written inline again and again.
There are no shared support modules for browser specs, tests/db checks, web formatting or route dependencies; otherwise the layout follows DH-03.
One architecture throughout, but client data access, run-tree scoping and snapshot reading are each solved several different ways.
Comments name each copy's partner, which made every copy easy to find, but they stand in for shared code.
Generated parsers guard most success bodies, but error bodies, run and session acceptances, the frozen policy snapshot and 25 UI label tables are cast or keyed by plain string.
Server errors share one ErrorResponse, but the browser re-reads it per screen, and lost-reply handling for paid admission exists in one of three flows.
Coverage is broad, but helpers are copied and drift: leak scans of different breadth, unguarded output parsing, and 36 sign-in copies.
Most duplication is signposted and mechanical to extract, but several copies guard secrets, money and state, and they have already diverged.

strengths.title: One shared provider HTTP module
strengths.evidence: services/agent/src/autobots/adapters/provider_http.py:43-83 holds one client factory (no redirects, trust_env=False), one status-to-failure-code map and one text budget, used by tavily.py:47, jina.py:47 and market_data.py:83 and :121. It is the model for the GitHub adapters.

strengths.title: The ownership guard lives inside the shared teardown
strengths.evidence: scripts/disposable_db.py:266-278: remove_stack re-checks project identity and labels before removing anything, so all 15 copied stack lifecycles inherit the guard; Cases (disposable_db.py:335) is the one result recorder for scripts.

strengths.title: A typed loader hook worth promoting
strengths.evidence: apps/web/components/tool-catalog.tsx:156-181: useLoaded<T>(path, parse) returns a loading, unavailable or ready state and aborts on unmount. It is used three times in that file and nowhere else.

strengths.evidence: apps/web/components/provider-settings-panel.tsx:19-64 keys its tables by generated types, e.g. Record<ProviderStatus["auth_status"], string>, so a new enum value fails compilation; 25 other tables in components use Record<string, string>.

strengths.evidence: tests/harness/test_shared_form_controls.py:13-23 fails when any screen draws a raw input, select or textarea; it also checks that it still scans enough files and that it would catch a raw control. The same pattern can guard the new shared helpers.

locations.note: public_text's pattern: only sk-, Bearer and JWT

findings.evidence: run_projection.py:59-61 matches only `sk-…`, `Bearer …` and `eyJ…` tokens. logs.py:12-24, under the comment 'Tool providers' keys, Decision 0017', also matches `tvly-`, `jina_`, `ghp_`/`gho_`…, `github_pat_`, credentialed postgres and https URLs, and `password=`-style pairs. evidence.py:35-40 carries the same comment and the same token families. I compiled both service patterns from their source and ran them on synthetic strings. public_text left a tvly- key, a jina_ key, a ghp_ token, a github_pat_ token and a postgresql://user:pw@… URL visible; logs.redact redacted all five.
findings.impact: The rule 'a key the model was shown is never displayed' (comment at run_projection.py:58; python-worker rule on sanitized public projections) was updated in two copies when Decision 0017 added tool keys, but not in the third. Approval arguments, run goals, search titles and memory snippets shown to every workspace member can therefore display a provider token that the logs would hide. Every new key family must be added in three places.
findings.recommendation: Keep one stdlib-only module of secret token families and credential shapes, compiled into the strictest union, and use it in both operations/logs.py and public_text. scripts/evidence.py runs under the system interpreter, so it keeps its own copy, plus a harness test that fails when its families differ from the shared module. This only widens public_text; never narrow any copy.

findings.impact: Run admission is a paid path. In the composer and the session panel (whose button at session-panel.tsx:190 is gated only by `ready`), a double click starts two billed runs. So does a retry after a lost reply, or after the BFF's 503 that follows a slow admission which already committed. continue-run, the third copy of the same request, handles both cases. findings.recommendation: Extract one admission client (startRun and startSession, built on the generated admitRun and createWorkSession) and one submit hook that holds the idempotency key until a definite answer and exposes a pending state. Use continue-run's rule: a success or a 4xx refusal clears the key; a lost reply or a 5xx keeps it. Map admission refusal codes to wording in one table, and use all of this from the composer, the session panel and continue-run.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: disable duplicate submits, with server idempotency as the correctness mechanism; AGENTS.md paid-call boundaries. Server idempotency remains the mechanism; the UI only stops minting a new key when the outcome is unknown.
findings.verifierNote: Re-read all three admissions: only continue-run.tsx keeps its key (line 39) and disables while pending; the composer's Run button (591-593) and the session panel's (190) stay enabled in flight, and bff.ts:102 times out at 30 s. findings.impact: Every screen re-decides cancellation, caching, parsing, failure reading and idempotency headers. The 'read an unread refusal' rule is applied in 16 places and skipped elsewhere. The browser uses none of the 78 generated request functions (the server uses 4), because runtime.requestJson discards the error body that screens need for code-specific messages. Changing a cross-cutting behavior such as timeouts, CSRF or error parsing means editing about 30 files.
findings.recommendation: Make the generated client usable in the browser: have runtime.requestJson throw a typed ApiFailure that carries the status and the error body, and accept per-call headers (or build ClientOptions per call). Add apps/web/lib/api.ts with browser ClientOptions (base URL '/api', CSRF-aware fetch, no-store, failed bodies drained), and move useLoaded from tool-catalog.tsx into lib as the one loader hook. Migrate screens as they are touched, and add a harness test like test_shared_form_controls.py that forbids new raw fetch( calls in components.
findings.ruleCheck: nextjs.md and DH-06: generated API types plus runtime parsing at untrusted boundaries, with explicit loading and unavailable states. runtime.ts is hand-written and in scope; generated.ts is only regenerated. Next.js stays a UI and BFF, and no business state moves into the browser.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted with git grep: 45 fetch( and 29 csrfFetch( calls in 31 component files, and 29 cancellation flags in 24 files. Failed-body drains are 16, not 14 (18 `.text()` calls, two of which read a file or a reply's content). The cited loaders and runtime.ts:157-172 match.

Outside frozen_policy, the snapshot is read by hand at 8 sites: goal_loop.py:586 and :598, browse_trial.py:202, and run_projection.py:251, :281-291, :428, :445 and :586.
findings.impact: The snapshot is the immutable record of which models a run may use; the model-gateway rule says role policy is frozen at admission. Its JSON shape is implicit: the writer and the validating reader live in different modules. goal_loop's two readers decide routing from raw dict access with neither validation nor the routes check, and browse_trial asserts on the raw dict before it validates. The shape has already changed once (sources) without a format version, because `version` holds ROLE_POLICY_VERSION. A further change must be mirrored in Python dict access and in SQL JSON paths, none of which a type checks.
findings.recommendation: Define the snapshot's stored shape once, beside the other row shapes, with encode and decode functions that accept every historical shape. Route all Python readers through decode, via a read_frozen_policy(connection, run_id) helper. Keep run_projection's SQL JSON paths, but name the key once and add a test that encode writes it. Add an explicit format version at the next shape change.

findings.title: Run spend and 'run plus descendants' are rewritten in SQL text, with two tree definitions that disagree

locations.note: _SELECT_RUN: spent and reserved
Run list: spent, reserved, unreported
Third copy: 'as the run list counts it (RN-01)'
OUTSTANDING, the status set the SQL copies restate as text
outstanding(): counts calls by run_id or root_run_id, but effects by recursive subtree
Recursive subtree CTE; repeated at :47 and :78
child_levels = 2, so grandchild runs exist
Fourth ledger copy, scoped by root_run_id only

findings.evidence:
There are 4 copies of the ledger SQL, 4 of the subtree CTE, and 12 lines using the `run_id = X or root_run_id = X` scope (grep).
```
# recovery.py:44 and :50-53
"from app_private.model_invocations where (run_id = %s or root_run_id = %s) "
"with recursive tree as (select id from public.runs where id = %s union all "
"select r.id from public.runs r join tree t on r.parent_run_id = t.id) "
"select count(*) from app_private.tool_receipts "
"where run_id in (select id from tree) and status = 'unknown'",
```
findings.impact: Children inherit the top root (assignments.py:79 and :134), so for a depth-1 child X with its own child, `run_id = X or root_run_id = X` matches only X's own calls while the recursive CTE matches X's whole subtree, and outstanding() mixes the two for verification (verification.py:43) and resume gating (assignments.py:285). Whether a mid-level run can then pass verification with a grandchild's uncertain call still open is not established: each level checks its direct child when resuming, and the top root counts every descendant through root_run_id. The ledger's status set also appears as SQL text in four places beside the OUTSTANDING constant that admission uses, so a new invocation status would change enforcement but not the figures screens show.
findings.recommendation: Name each scope once and choose deliberately: one subtree helper (a Python SQL fragment, or a SQL function added by a forward migration) and one ledger helper. Build the ledger columns from model_admission.OUTSTANDING passed as a parameter, as admission already does. Then decide, with a disposable-database test using depth-2 delegation, which scope outstanding() should count calls in.
